boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Salineville record (July 26, 1863) in Morgan's Raid in Kentucky, Indiana, and Ohio [July 1863]. Major Way's morning fight and the surrender near New Lisbon the same afternoon are both within the day; which the frozen record covers is not established. The raid's start strength, detachments, captures and campaign effects span July 2–26 and several engagements; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen field reads 3,000 (US 2,600; CS 400). NPS says Morgan escaped Buffington with about 400 men. Duke, not an eyewitness of these days, says the two reorganized brigades were each a little more than 400 strong and that a fresh disaster on the 26th reduced the command to 250 men. Shackelford says he resumed the chase with 500 men on July 21, that Major Rue brought about 375 fresh men, and that Morgan crossed the railroad with about 400 men after Way's fight.
claims.rationale: Figures differ in time and population; none is adopted as matched opening strength. Duke's '2Gth' is an OCR reading.

claims.value: Duke says Morgan formally surrendered to Captain Burbeck of the Ohio militia on condition of parole, and that Shackelford, on arriving, disapproved the arrangement and prevented it. Shackelford says Burnside had placed him in command of all troops in the pursuit, that Major Rue properly refused to act until he came up, and that he regarded the surrender to a militia captain as unfair and illegal and would not recognize it. The frozen commanders are Shackelford and Morgan, both Brigadier Generals.
claims.rationale: The validity of the Burbeck surrender is disputed by the two interested accounts; the frozen commanders do not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: NPS says that during the raid Morgan's men captured and paroled about 6,000 Union soldiers and militia, destroyed 34 bridges and diverted tens of thousands of troops. Duke judges the raid's objects accomplished, thinks it delayed the fall of East Tennessee, and says it destroyed Morgan's division.
claims.rationale: Raid-wide claims and an interested participant's campaign judgment; not a tactical result of this record, not assigned to any engagement and not a causal estimate.

open_questions: Way's and Rue's reports, Burbeck's account and the scope of the frozen 364 remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Duke's History of Morgan's Cavalry (1867) is an interested Confederate participant history: Duke commanded a brigade on the raid by his own account and was captured at Buffington, so his account of later days is not eyewitness. The Burnside, Hobson and Shackelford reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXIII, Part 1, are interested Union accounts. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
